title: Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan
hook: a grammar teacher whose every lesson turns into Krishna

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai's songs counted a treasure that grows when it's spent. What did you spend? Day nine hundred thirty-three.

A grammar teacher in Bengal has a problem. His students come to learn Sanskrit grammar, and every rule he explains turns into Krishna. A verb ending? Krishna. A noun? One of Krishna's names. Tradition says this young teacher, called Nimai, was known in his town of Navadvipa as a brilliant scholar and a fierce debater. Then he went on pilgrimage to Gaya, and came home unable to talk about anything else. His students, the story goes, finally closed their books and left. He let them go. He had found something louder than grammar.
screen: `A GRAMMAR TEACHER IN BENGAL.` → `EVERY RULE TURNS INTO KRISHNA.` → `THE STUDENTS CLOSE THEIR BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Nimai is the man remembered as Chaitanya. Back home, he and his friends began to gather at night in the courtyard of a devotee named Shrivasa, doors shut, singing God's names together. Drums, hand cymbals, one voice leading and everyone answering. That's kirtan: praise sung out loud, together, the names repeated again and again. Then the doors opened. Chaitanya's companions took the singing into the lanes of Navadvipa, a procession of drums and cymbals moving from house to house, and whoever heard it could fall in behind. At the center of it, his tradition places one chant: Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Nothing but names, calling and calling. What's radical is how little it asks. No Sanskrit grammar. No years of study. No temple door to get through. You need a voice, or even just ears and the willingness to answer the line that's sung to you. A scholar who could out-argue his town set down the argument and picked up the drum. His followers in Bengal, the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, remember him dancing as he sang, weeping, falling to the ground, his whole body caught up in the names. They also hold that he was more than a saint: Krishna himself, joined with Radha, come to taste his own love from the inside. Others honor him as a great teacher of devotion. Either way, what he gave the street was the same: a song anyone could join on the first try.
screen: `NIGHTS IN SHRIVASA'S COURTYARD.` · `THE DOORS OPEN TO THE LANES.` · `NOTHING BUT NAMES.` · then, large: `A SONG ANYONE CAN JOIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath find its rhythm. Kirtan is a call and an answer, so let your breath do both. The out-breath is the leader's line. The in-breath is the crowd, answering. If you'd like, hum softly on the out-breath, or whisper a name that matters to you, and let the in-breath be the pause where the answer comes back. If you pray, you can use a name of God you already know. If not, a single soft sound is enough. Keep the call and answer going, gently. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan. Praise sung aloud, God's names repeated together with drums and cymbals, which Chaitanya took out of a closed courtyard and into the street.
Your line: a song anyone can join. Today, join something you'd usually only watch: a song, a chorus, a cheer, even one line of it. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: In Gaudiya Vaishnava temples and homes, kirtan is sung with drums and hand cymbals, one voice leading and the group answering, and street processions of chanting, called nagar kirtan, still pass through towns and cities.

fork.setup: you're a celebrated young scholar, home from pilgrimage, and all you can talk about is Krishna. your students want grammar. what do you do?
options: go back to teaching grammar as before.
let the students go, and start singing the names.
write a learned book proving Krishna is in grammar.
fork.reveal: tradition says the students left and Nimai let them go. the nights of singing in Shrivasa's courtyard came next, and then the street.

original.note: Sanskrit and Hindi, in Devanagari: praise sung aloud, God's names sung together.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hare Krishna is a chant you've heard on a city sidewalk.
what it means: a chant of names that Chaitanya's tradition placed at the heart of kirtan, sung by anyone who answers.
what a scholar hears: the chant is found in the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, and the Bengali lives of Chaitanya tell of the closed-door nights at Shrivasa's house before the singing took to the streets.

sources.ref: Chaitanya Charitamrita, Adi-lila, Nimai's life in Navadvipa, his return from Gaya, and kirtan at Shrivasa's house

Chaitanya Bhagavata of Vrindavana Dasa, Madhya-khanda, Nimai's return from Gaya and the closing of his school

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the account of Nimai's grammar lessons turning to Krishna after Gaya and the students leaving (told in the Chaitanya Bhagavata and Chaitanya Charitamrita); confirm which text is best cited.

The mahamantra is spoken in the order used in Gaudiya practice (Hare Krishna first). The Kali-Santarana Upanishad gives it with Hare Rama first; a Keeper should confirm how to present the order and the citation.
Gaudiya belief that Chaitanya is Krishna together with Radha is attributed to that tradition; 'Others honor him as a great teacher of devotion' is meant to avoid ranking. Confirm.
Trapdoor floor one mentions airports and sidewalks; confirm the tone is respectful of the modern Hare Krishna movement (ISKCON).
howItsDone: confirm 'nagar kirtan' as the term for street processions in this tradition.
